newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich says White House, Congress close on budget.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich says White House, Congress close on budget.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich said only minor issues remained to be resolved in budget talks between the White House and Congress, predicting that a final deal was possible on Sunday "if we're lucky."
"I think we have an agreement, it's never done until it's done," Gingrich said as Republicans and administration officials prepared for another round of negotiations in the Capitol.
The Georgia Republican said the two sides were down to three "tiny" tax and spending issues, but was not specific.

Congressional aides cautioned that while agreement appeared very close, some tough work remained to clinch budget and tax cut legislation that could pass Congress by Republican leaders' Aug. 1 deadline.
Congressional sources said both sides had made concessions on thorny tax issues over the past several days.

In a key area under dispute, the White House is willing to agree that a $500-per-child tax credit would be available for teenagers as well as younger children and let families making more than $60,000 receive the full credit, a source said.
Republicans seemed to be moving to allow low-income families to receive the credit based upon their payroll tax as well as their federal income taxes, a White House demand.
Republicans appeared ready to give the president more than $16 billion for the proposed child health care programme to cover poor children without health insurance, the source said.

Earlier Sunday, House Majority Leader Dick Armey signalled Republicans may be willing to abandon one of their top issues -- indexing of capital gains tax rates to save investors from paying tax on profits due to inflation -- in order to get a tax bill Clinton will sign into law.

"We understand that in order to get some of the other things that may not be something to hold up," Armey, a Texas Republican, said on ABC's "This Week." "I'll have a chance next year with another tax package to maybe pick up those pieces that get lost behind in this one," he added.
The Senate's top Republican said chances were good they could reach the tax and spending deal if President Bill Clinton would become personally involved.

"We're at a point after a meeting ended last night about 6:30 (2230 GMT) where the president needs to step in and say 'yes, this is important, we're not going to use this for political position, we're going to do what's right for the country'," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said on NBC's "Meet the Press" programme.
"If the president will do that, if he'll join with us, we can make it happen. But right now, we're so close and yet so far away," the Mississippi Republican said.
Gingrich said White House officials had briefed him and Lott on Sunday morning.

As the president prepared to play golf in Los Angeles, the White House said he was "fully engaged" through his negotiating team. "At the appropriate time he would be willing to get personally involved in the talks," presidential spokesman Joe Lockhart said.

The White House said last week that the president was ready to give up his scheduled August vacation in Martha's Vineyard, Mass., to finish up the tax and spending deals. Congressional Republican leaders have said they want to strike a deal before leaving for vacation on Aug. 1.
Clinton's team also includes Budget Director Franklin Raines, Economic adviser Gene Sperling and congressional liaison John Hilley.
Raines, appearing on "Meet the Press" repeated the president's view that indexing of tax rates would lead to a veto of the entire tax cut bill.

Administration officials and top Republicans, led by Gingrich and Lott have closeted themselves in a private third floor meeting room of the Capitol out of bounds of the press in order to hammer out a deal. Most Democrats, including House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri and Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota, have not been included in the negotiations.
